::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Essay, November 2026.** A short, personal essay. It starts from a news story about Kurt Gödel's notebooks, read with the help of AI. And it starts from a small experiment of my own, run on two ordinary processor cores. It asks a plain question: to discover something, do we really need huge machines? The first figure is a schematic of my own. The second shows the numbers of my experiment, which are preliminary. The code that draws both is linked under them.
:::

**In short.** This week I read that an AI helped a logician go through more than a thousand pages of Gödel's notebooks. Together they found hundreds of results nobody had studied. It made me think. Gödel found what he found with a pencil. Turing too. Today we talk as if every discovery needs a data centre. I don't think so. I had an idea about how a network could think: as a ball rolling in a landscape. I tested it on two processor cores, with an AI assistant helping me write the code. The small test already showed something surprising. Big machines still matter: to check a result, and to read what no person has time to read. But they come second. First comes the idea, and a small test is often enough to start.

## 1. A notebook nobody could read

A few days ago I came across a post on LinkedIn. It said that an AI, Anthropic's Claude, had helped decode Kurt Gödel's old notebooks. Hundreds of theorems, hidden for almost a century.

I wanted the real story, so I looked it up. Here is what was reported [@aitldr2026; @archyde2026]. In the early 1940s, Gödel filled sixteen notebooks, about 1,009 pages, with mathematics and logic. He wrote much of it in Gabelsberger, an old German shorthand that almost nobody reads any more. Since 2017, the logician Jan von Plato, in Helsinki, has studied them.

The detail I like most is this one. The AI did not read the shorthand. Von Plato did. He taught himself the shorthand, transcribed the pages, and wrote six books about Gödel. Then he gave all of it to the AI. It came back with a long explanation of the notebooks and a list of 663 results that Gödel had proved, sketched or outlined. Checked with a proof assistant, a program that verifies every step of a proof, about 400 held as stated. About 200 needed a repair, and about 50 were wrong. Gödel had sometimes marked his own notes as wrong, so that last part is not a surprise.

There is also one result that stands out. As reported, Gödel came very close to something Paul Cohen proved in 1963. It is about one of the basic rules of set theory, the axiom of choice: it can be neither proved nor refuted from the others. Gödel claimed later in life that he had found it in the 1940s. The notebooks seem to show he was one definition away.

I should correct one thing the post said, because it matters. Gödel did not prove the continuum hypothesis. Around 1940 he showed that it cannot be *disproved* from the usual rules of mathematics [@godel1940]. In 1963 Cohen showed that it cannot be *proved* either [@cohen1963]. That earned him the Fields Medal. The two halves together say: the question is open, by nature.

## 2. What a mind did with almost nothing

Now, look at what Gödel had. Paper, a pencil, and a way of writing so private that it took a man years to learn it again.

With that, in 1931, he showed that mathematics can never be complete: in any honest system strong enough to count, there are true statements it cannot prove [@godel1931]. Five years later, Alan Turing used the same kind of thinking to describe a machine that can compute anything computable. And he showed that some problems no machine can ever solve [@turing1937]. The whole theory of the computer you are reading this on came out of that.

No data centre. No graphics cards. Not even a computer, because the computer did not exist yet. They were the ones who imagined it.

That is the thought that stayed with me after the news. Today we talk as if discovery needs a huge machine and the power of a small town. Decades ago, minds found almost everything we now build on, with almost nothing. AI will surely take us to a next level, and we will use it. But do we absolutely need it? I wanted to test that question on myself.

## 3. My own small test

I am not a researcher in machine learning. But I had an idea that would not leave me.

When a language model reads a text, it uses a step called attention. Each word looks at the other words and pulls in what it needs. I kept seeing that step as a landscape. Each fact in the text digs a well. The question is a ball. One step of attention is the ball moving once towards the right well. This picture is not only mine: researchers showed in 2020 that one attention step is exactly one step of a kind of memory network built on wells [@ramsauer2021].

So I asked a simple question. Why stop after one step? Let the ball roll until it rests. And let the text itself shape the landscape, new for every text.

![**Figure 1.** The picture behind my experiment. Each fact in the text digs a well; the question is a ball that starts in one well and rolls, hop by hop, from A to B, to C, to D, where it settles on the answer. The landscape is rebuilt for every new text. Schematic, my own; code in [figs.py](figs.py).](figures/fig01.svg){fig-alt="A black curved line forms a landscape with four wells labelled A, B, C and D, over a light amber fill. An amber ball sits in well A, labelled: the question starts here. Dashed amber arrows jump from A to B, B to C and C to D, labelled hop 1, hop 2 and hop 3. Well D is labelled: it settles, the answer. The title reads: each fact in the text digs a well, the question is a ball, let it roll until it rests."}

To test it, I used a simple task. The text is a list of pairs of random symbols: A points to B, B points to C, and so on. The question gives a start. The network must follow the chain to its end. Each link is one hop. The symbols change every time, so the network cannot memorise the answers. It has to learn how to follow.

Now I must be honest about how this was built. The idea, the landscape and the ball, is mine. But an AI assistant helped me write the code, run the tests and write the research plan. Without it, this would have taken me months of evenings, not a few days. So I did use AI. What I did not use is a big machine. Everything ran on two ordinary processor cores. The networks are tiny: between 50,000 and 90,000 numbers to learn. The large language models people talk about have hundreds of billions. A single training run took a few minutes.

## 4. What the small machine found

The first result was a failure, and I learned more from it than from the successes.

The network found the right answer, then rolled past it. At the step it was trained for, the answer was there. If I let it roll sixteen times longer, it was right only one time in five. The answer was not a place where the ball rests. It was a place the ball passes by. Researchers call this overthinking, and it is well known in networks that repeat the same step [@bansal2022]. The fix is also known: keep the question inside the landscape, not only at the start. With that change, the ball stayed on the right answer, even after rolling sixteen times longer, and even when it started from a random place.

Then came the surprise. I trained the network on chains of one to three hops only. Then I gave it longer chains, which it had never seen. With four hops, it was right 94% of the time. With five hops, 77%. A standard attention network with three or five layers got none of them right.

Was it the rolling, or the way the wells are dug? I made a cleaner test. Same network, same code, one change. In one version, each well is dug on its own, independently of the others. In the other version, the wells compete, the way they do in normal attention: if one gets deeper, the others get shallower. Both versions learned the training chains equally well. On longer chains, they split.

![**Figure 2.** Same network, one change. Trained on chains of one to three hops, tested on four and five. With independent wells, 81% and 58% correct; with competing wells, 32% and 3%. Two training runs each, on two processor cores: a preliminary result, not yet confirmed. Data from my own experiment; code in [figs.py](figs.py).](figures/fig02.svg){fig-alt="A line chart of correct answers in percent against the number of hops in the chain, from 1 to 5. Hops 1 to 3 are shaded and labelled trained on 1 to 3 hops. Two lines start together near 100 percent and stay close up to 3 hops, about 94 percent. Then the amber line, independent wells, falls gently to 81 percent at 4 hops and 58 percent at 5. The blue line, competing wells, drops to 32 percent at 4 hops and 3 percent at 5."}

With independent wells, the network was right 81% of the time on four hops and 58% on five. With competing wells, 32% and 3%. I think I understand why. When the wells compete, the ball always feels a mix of all of them. When they are independent, it can listen only to the well it is sitting in, and then move on to the next one.

I want to be careful here. This is two training runs, on a toy task, with tiny networks. It may not hold at a larger scale. But it is a real difference, found with almost nothing.

## 5. The objection: then is not now

There is a strong answer to everything I just wrote, and I want to give it its full weight.

It goes like this. Gödel and Turing worked on empty ground. The big, simple discoveries were still there to be found. Today, the easy ground is taken. And in AI itself, history has been harsh with clever ideas. The researcher Richard Sutton called it the bitter lesson: over seventy years, methods that simply used more computing power beat methods built on human insight, again and again [@sutton2019]. Language models did not come from a beautiful idea about wells. They came from scale. Seen that way, my two cores are nostalgia.

I think that is partly right. But I think it mixes up two moments: when an idea is born, and when it is proven to win.

The bitter lesson is about who wins at the end, on the big benchmarks. It says little about where ideas come from. Attention itself began as an idea in a paper on translation, years before anyone spent millions on it [@bahdanau2015]. Scale makes good ideas strong. It does not tell you which idea to scale.

And the Gödel story, read closely, says the same. The hardest step was not done by the machine. A man spent years learning a dead shorthand, by hand, so the pages could be read at all. The machine then did what no single person has time to do: read everything, connect it, list it. It made weeks out of what would have been a lifetime. That is a huge help. But it came second.

My own experiment shows the other side too, and I should say it. My small result could vanish. The next step in my plan is a test on a real graphics card, with five runs per model instead of two, and properly tuned rivals. If the gap closes, my idea was wrong, and I will need a bigger machine to know it. So the honest claim is not that we never need big machines. It is this: we don't always need them, and we don't need them first.

The same goes for AI itself. I used an AI assistant, and it saved me months. But I did not need it to have the idea. The picture of the ball in the landscape came on its own, the old way, in my head.

## 6. What I take from it

So here is the order I now believe in. First the idea, from a mind, with almost nothing. Then a small test that could prove it wrong. Then, only if it survives, a big machine to check it and to scale it.

Before reaching for a data centre, there is one question worth asking: what is the smallest test that could tell me I am wrong? Very often, it fits on a laptop. Gödel's fits in a notebook.

AI will take us further. I am sure of that, and I am glad of it. It reads what we have no time to read, and it builds what we have no time to build. But it still needs someone to bring it a question worth asking.

Gödel had a pencil. I had two cores and an idea. The pencil came first. It still does.
